en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Ānanda said: "Thus have I heard. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "There are those who serve the Buddha and obtain..."
Those who possess wealth and status find harmony and union, while those who suffer decline and loss do not find harmony and union; why is there this inequality?
We pray that the Buddha, the God among Gods, will explain this for us all.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are those who revere the Buddha, receive the precepts from a master of illumination, do not lose their vigor in practicing what they have received, perform prostrations morning and evening, reverently light lamps, observe the fasts without weariness, and keep their minds constantly joyful, then they will be protected by benevolent deities. Whatever they undertake will meet with success, their hundred affairs will increase twofold, and they will be honored by devas, nāgas, spirits, and all people;
in the end, they will surely attain the Way. Such good men and good women are true disciples of the Buddha."

"There are those who serve the Buddha but do not encounter a good teacher, nor do they see the scriptural teachings; their faith is not firm, and though they bear the name of 'precept-keeper,' they violate the true discipline.

Since there are no images, they neither burn incense, light lamps, nor perform prostrations; they constantly harbor anger and use foul language to revile others. They do not observe the six fast days and take up the killing of living beings with their own hands.

They do not respect the Buddhist scriptures, placing them in miscellaneous boxes or among worn-out items, or keeping them on the beds of their wives and children in impure places; or they hang them on walls where there is no altar or platform, treating them no differently than worldly books."

If one suffers from illness and completely fails to recite the Buddha's name, instead summoning shamans to perform divinations and sacrifices, and entreating malevolent spirits, the celestial deities will remain distant and unable to provide protection; demons and specters will advance daily, and evil ghosts will block the gates, causing one’s resources to dwindle and every endeavor to meet with failure.

Those who commit sins in the present life are not disciples of the Buddha; upon death, they enter the hells (*niraya*) where they are tortured by a hundred poisons, and the agony of their spirits is so extreme that it is beyond words.

These fools, clouded by ignorance, are unable to reflect upon themselves; though they have previously failed to cultivate merit, they instead resent Heaven and Earth. Blaming the sages and faulting Heaven, they remain thus deluded and confused. This is the height of folly, and they consequently become bound and entangled within the three miserable realms (*trāya*).

“O Lady, those who attain the Way all do so by arising from goodness. With the sutras and precepts as one’s own guide, one restrains the mind, body, and speech; goodness serves as a great armor against the fear of weapons, and goodness serves as a great ship for crossing over rivers and deep pools. One who is able to maintain faith will find peace and harmony within the household.”
In this present life, there are blessings and fortunes that follow naturally; one receives retribution for what they do, which is not bestowed by a deity.

If a person does not believe and does not uphold the sutras and precepts, their future existence will become increasingly dire. Good and evil follow a person like a shadow follows a form; do not harbor doubts, lest you fall into the evil realms yourself, from which it is truly difficult to escape.
If you believe with sincerity and do not transgress, you will always find peace wherever you are;
the Buddha’s words are most truthful and never deceive anyone.

A Buddha’s world is difficult to encounter and a human body is difficult to obtain; now that you serve the Buddha, your past merit is great. You should contemplate repaying this kindness by proclaiming the teachings of the Dharma, extensively cultivating fields of merit, and practicing until you attain liberation; then, wherever you go, there shall be no sorrow.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a person does not kill with their own hand but instructs another to kill, what is their offense?
Is there no offense?”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! To instruct another to kill is more grave than to kill on one’s own.”
Why is this? It may be that they are slaves or persons of low station who harbor no intent to kill;
or it may be that they are coerced by kings or government officials, acting on their behalf without any intention of their own.

To instruct others in killing, knowing full well that one is committing a transgression, to plot maliciously to harm others while shifting the blame onto them, and to deceive the Triple Gem while betraying the natural order—there is no sin greater than this.
Such enmity will be requited, leading to calamities endured life after life without end.

In this present life there is no peace, and after death one enters hell, where one suffers agonizing, tearing pain. Upon emerging from hell, one becomes an animal, being slaughtered and disemboweled, with skin and bones exposed as one’s flesh is used to repay others. All of this results from having committed acts of cruelty, violence, and rebellion in previous lives, plundering and harming sentient beings through secret plots and malice, devoid of any heart of compassion.
"To see someone killing another and to rejoice in their place, finding greater pleasure in it than in killing oneself—
the gravity of such a sin is as profound as this. Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying,

"As for those people in the world and the disciples of the Buddha who treat their teacher with contempt, harbor ill will toward their teacher and toward those of moral virtue— what is their transgression?"
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!
As a person, one should love and delight in the virtues of others and rejoice in the goodness of others; one must not be envious of them.”
To harbor ill will toward one's teacher or a person of moral virtue is no different from harboring ill will toward the Buddha.
Would it not be painful to take a crossbow weighing ten thousand *shi* and turn it upon one's own body?
Ānanda said: “It is most painful, most painful,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"If a person harbors an evil intention toward one who possesses the Way and its virtue, or toward their teacher, the pain will be more intense than being shot by a crossbow.
As a disciple, one must not treat one's teacher with contempt or harbor an evil intention toward those who possess the Way and its virtue."
One should regard those who possess moral virtue as Buddhas and must not harbor envy or slander them.
When a person possesses the virtue of the precepts, they move the hearts of the devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, all of whom revere and honor them.
It would be better to cast one's body into fire or have one's flesh cut by a sharp blade than to harbor jealousy or slander this virtuous person;
the sin of such an act is no small matter. Be careful! Be careful!
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May a teacher reprimand a disciple, magnifying a minor offense into a major one, even when there is no offense? May he do so without transgression?"
The Buddha said: "It must not be! It must not be!"
The relationship between teacher and disciple is one where righteousness moves spontaneously; they should trust one another deeply and regard each other as themselves.

What one does not practice oneself, one must not impose upon others. One should exalt the codes of propriety and law, instructing them through the Way, so that they may be harmonious, loyal, and steadfast, never harboring resentment or engaging in litigation.

Between disciple and teacher, there are two principles of sincerity: the teacher should act as a teacher, and the disciple should act as a disciple. Do not slander one another; be careful not to harbor malice, for even a small resentment can grow into something great and burn you yourself.

Observe the evil people and demonic bhikṣus of this world: their teachers are not true teachers and their disciples are not true disciples; they do nothing but practice evil together and have no thought for the path of cultivation.

Those who ruin their own goodness covet worldly occupations; disregarding impermanence, they accumulate wealth only to bring about their own ruin. After death, they fall into the evil realms as hungry ghosts or animals, never having been treated with such regard as one would a cow. Seeking nothing in this world, how can you fail to contemplate repaying the Buddha’s kindness?
One should uphold the sutras and precepts, leading one another by means of the Way.

The Way must be studied; the sutras must be read; goodness must be practiced. By practicing goodness and spreading virtue, one delivers the spirit from suffering, transcends birth and death, and does not treat the worthy with arrogance nor slander the good. One should not use a minor transgression to prove a person guilty of a great crime. To violate the law and lose the principle of reason is a crime of no small magnitude; there is evidence for both sin and merit.
"How terrifying!
How terrifying!
Ānanda spoke again to the Buddha, saying:

“Disciples in the final age will be born into this realm of Māra, where there are many causes and conditions, such as the pursuit of domestic life and the burdens of body and speech; how, then, should they practice?”

The Buddha said: "As a disciple of the Buddha, although there may be causes and conditions [for transgression], you must uphold the precepts without violation. With sincerity, faith, awe, and caution, take refuge in the Triple Gem; serve your two parents with filial piety; be diligent and virtuous toward both internal and external relations; do not harbor deceitful thoughts, ensuring that mind and speech correspond; employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and know the proper time for advancing or retreating. In this way, one may engage in worldly affairs, but one must not harbor worldly intentions."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"What is meant by 'worldly matters,' and what is meant by 'worldly intentions'?"
The Buddha said:

“As a disciple of the Buddha, one may engage in the business of trade for profit, provided that one uses measures, scales, and cubits fairly and according to principle. One must not be crooked or craftily deceitful in order to encroach upon others. Funerary rites, moving house, marriages, and betrothals—these are worldly affairs.”

Regarding worldly concerns, as a disciple of the Buddha, one must not practice divination, request talismans or incantations for spirits, perform sacrifices, offer prayers for deliverance from calamities, or harbor superstitious fears regarding inauspiciousness.

Those who receive the Buddha’s five precepts are persons of merit and virtue; they have nothing to fear or avoid. Whatever they undertake to perform, they should inform the Triple Gem, and there will be no action that does not lead to auspiciousness.
For those whose virtue lies in the precepts, the protection of the Way is their strength; there are no devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits who do not revere and submit to them.
When the precepts are honored, one is revered; wherever they go, they are always at peace.
Those who do not attain [this understanding] create obstacles for themselves.

Good and evil arise from the mind; calamity and fortune depend on the person. They follow like a shadow pursuing a form, or an echo responding to a sound. Heaven covers all, and earth supports all. The virtue of preceptual practice brings about blessings naturally;

celestial deities provide protection, moving the ten directions. Their merit becomes equal to that of the heavens, and their achievements are so lofty that the various sages sigh in admiration, finding them difficult to measure. The wise man understands destiny and remains upright throughout his life; knowing well the Buddha’s teachings, he attains the path to transcend the world.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, Ānanda adjusted his *kāṣāya* robe, touched his head to the ground, and said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!

We are fortunate to be near the Tathāgata and to drink the flavor of the Dharma with our own ears. Your universal kindness and great compassion take pity on all beings; you have raised up a field of merit so that they may be delivered from suffering."

The Buddha’s words are sincere, yet those who believe them are few; this world abounds in evil, and sentient beings curse one another. They place great trust in ghosts and spirits, turning their backs on the right path and following what is perverse. Thus, the heavens are all empty while hell is filled to overflowing—how truly lamentable!
If there are those with faith—whether one or two—how lamentable that the world is decaying to such an extent!
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the sūtras and Dharma alone will remain, yet few will practice them;
the people will increasingly become hypocritical, gradually wasting away and falling into decline until they are extinguished.
Alas! How painful! What can we rely upon?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to manifest his transformative power for the sake of those who have recently begun their studies, and not yet enter parinirvāṇa.
Thereupon, Ānanda offered this verse:
“The Buddha is the protector of the three realms; His grace is vast, and his compassion is great.”
I pray that for the sake of those of us who have studied late, you will not yet enter *nirvāṇa*.
How painful it is for those who have not yet attained realization, who remain in a state of blinding ignorance and fail to distinguish the true from the false!
When the Dharma drum resounds throughout the three thousandfold world-system, how could they not hear it?
In this defiled age, various evil people, Falling back into their own perversions,
Do not believe that there is a Buddha in the world, And thus create the root of manifold transgressions for themselves.
When their lives end, they go to hell, Where swords and blades dismember their bodies.
Those who enjoy killing during sacrifices find boiling cauldrons surging within them;
those who are lewd embrace copper pillars while great fires burn them;
those who slander pure and noble sages have their tongues pulled out with iron hooks.
Those who drink wine to excess and lack propriety shall have molten copper poured into their mouths;
if they are reborn as humans, they will be dull-witted and devoid of moral principles.
By abstaining from killing, one attains long life, remains free from illness, and is always healthy and strong.
By not stealing, one will later become greatly wealthy, with money and goods always abundant;
by not committing sexual misconduct, one’s body will be fragrant and pure;
by being sincere and free from deceit, one will be trusted and relied upon by others.
Not intoxicated, one attains wisdom and is revered by all.
Transcending the five worldly blessings through the Dharma, one becomes a peer among devas and humans.
One’s rebirth shall be multiplied millions of times; the True Truth is most clearly manifest.
Foolish and ignorant, they fail to distinguish the Path; They obscure the Sages and revile the Perfectly Awakened One.
Upon death, they enter the Avīci Hell, With an iron wheel upon their heads.
Seeking death, they find no release; In an instant, their forms are transformed.
Spears and halberds pierce one another; bodies are hacked and severed.
In their dense ignorance they do not understand the truth; driven by evil, they bind and entangle one another.
They wander through the various realms of existence, taking on the forms of birds, beasts, and domestic livestock.
Being slaughtered and dismembered by others, one repays past enmity with flesh;
through unrighteousness, one falls into the evil realms, making liberation exceedingly difficult to seek.
Since a human body is so hard to obtain, and the Buddha-dharma is so hard to hear, [one must not waste this opportunity].
The World-Honored One is the benefactor of the multitudes, the most preeminent among those who dwell in peace.
He has spread forth the Dharma of ambrosia, which those of later learning universally practice;
out of compassion for us, he manifests profound wisdom, for he takes pity upon all living beings.
Awakening reveals the stages of the path; The practitioner attains liberation.
The person of merit moves ever forward; Seeing the Truth, they do not give rise to further birth.
I take refuge in the Peaceful, Benevolent, and Holy One, Who plants the seeds upon the path to the Deathless.
In benevolence and compassion, none surpass the Buddha, Whose divine and wondrous form manifests majestic radiance.
May all people be granted the opportunity to drink the nectar of immortality,
Ride the boat of wisdom to the further shore, And strike the Dharma-gong throughout the three thousandfold world.
He is free from the notion of self and mine; the World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma.
We have received this auspicious joy and attained the relinquishing of the twelve links of dependent origination.
With great delight we bow our heads in prostration, taking refuge in the Most Unsurpassed One.

After Ānanda had prostrated himself and recited these verses, the great assembly gathered there attained the stage of non-retrogression; their minds were opened and liberated, and they donned the great armor of *saṃnāha* with resolve for the Unsurpassed Way. The sound of the nectar-like Dharma permeated the ten directions like a fragrant incense.

Manifesting the stages of the path as a bridge for all, the king, his ministers, the people, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, having heard what the Buddha spoke and what Ānanda recited, were moved by both sorrow and inspiration, filled with both sighs and joy. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid homage to Ānanda, and departed after receiving his instructions.
The Sūtra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha Spoken by the Buddha at the Request of Ānanda.
